content.title: Trump and the threat from Russia force a change: Europe agrees on much higher military spending
content.lead: From two to five percent: NATO's new spending target represents a huge leap. What's behind this new percentage, and how far are NATO countries from achieving it?
content.author: Andreas Rüesch

content.author: Mindaugas Kulbis / AP

content.text: Just a few years ago, such news would have been sensational: All NATO members are spending at least two percent of their economic output (GDP) on defense this year, the alliance recently announced. NATO had been working toward this goal for two decades, primarily at the urging of the United States. Last year, only 22 of the 32 member states met the target. But no sooner has the goal been achieved than it is already considered inadequate. Russia's belligerent course makes it clear that the Western alliance must invest significantly more to regain its deterrent capability.

After US President Donald Trump called for a new 5% spending target at the World Economic Forum in Davos in January, intense debates raged within the alliance. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte initially proposed a 3% target. But now the discussions are over: the US prevailed; at the NATO summit at the end of June, the alliance announced the new 5% target. However, members are only required to spend 3.5% of their GDP on military expenditures; the remaining 1.5% can be allocated to militarily relevant infrastructure. This leaves room for some accounting maneuvering. Furthermore, there is a long transition period.

content.title: We're talking about trillions of dollars

content.text: But even military spending of 3.5 percent is an extremely ambitious target. According to NATO, only one country exceeded this last year – Poland, with 4.1 percent. Even the US, at 3.2 percent, failed to reach the required level. The European average was just over 2 percent. The provisional figures for 2025 do not paint a completely different picture: in addition to Poland, Lithuania and Latvia are now also above the 3.5 percent mark. However, the overall European average remains at around 2.2 percent.

Behind this abstract future target lie gigantic additional expenditures. According to the latest NATO statistics, the 30 European member states budgeted a total of around $560 billion for military spending this year. With a target of 3.5 percent of GDP, this translates to additional expenditures of approximately $330 billion per year. Over a decade, and with a steadily growing economy, these expenditures would accumulate to several trillion dollars. Political resistance to such burdens is already evident, even if governments are currently emphasizing their defense efforts.

A glance at the map of NATO territory below reveals a wide range of defense policy ambitions. Unsurprisingly, spending in 2024 was particularly high on NATO's eastern flank, often well above the two percent target. However, nine countries, in the west and south of the continent, still failed to meet the minimum requirement.

content.text: Spain stands out as being at the bottom of the list, having clearly missed NATO targets with military spending of less than 1.3 percent of GDP. According to provisional NATO figures for 2025, Spain has now suddenly cleared the 2 percent hurdle – as have Italy, Portugal, and the other laggards. However, this miraculous increase raises questions about its sustainability, and Spain has already made it clear that it will ignore the five percent target.

But everything is relative: If Switzerland were a member of NATO, it would be at the bottom of the rankings with a value of 0.7 percent. Poland and the Baltic states, on the other hand, can face the new target of 3.5 percent with equanimity. The situation is different for economic heavyweights like Germany and France, which only just barely reached the two percent target – and in Germany's case, only through budgetary maneuvering.

content.text: The two percent target, enshrined in 2014, was already frequently criticized, and a five percent target would be even more so. Her main objection is that a rigid budget target offers no guarantee of achieving the goal – making Europe safe. These percentages don't reveal how efficiently and effectively governments spend the money. Furthermore, not every euro serves collective security – France, for example, also uses its military to pursue its great power ambitions overseas. Different national budgeting methods further complicate comparisons.

But percentage targets are a means of driving policy. A comparison with the past is also illuminating: During the Cold War, much higher military spending was the norm for decades. Since a hot war is currently raging in Europe and NATO is facing its most serious threat in a long time, the comparative figures from that era are relevant.
As the graph below shows, in the 1970s the British spent around five percent, the French and Germans around three percent, and the Swiss two percent of their economic output on the military.

content.text: The figures for these countries only fell significantly after the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991. This reflected the desire for a «peace dividend.» In the case of Great Britain, Germany, and Switzerland, this amounted to roughly half of their previous military spending. Austerity measures continued everywhere until the 2010s, before increased funding for the armed forces began to flow again from 2020 onward.

content.title: Suddenly, 60 percent more combat brigades are needed

content.text: Now, spending curves are expected to rise sharply. This is not only a consequence of the change of power in the White House, but also of NATO's new defense plans. For the first time since the Cold War, as NATO's Supreme Allied Commander Europe, General Christopher Cavoli , put it, there are once again classic operational plans: These specify precisely how certain areas are to be defended and what resources are needed for this purpose.

In recent months, the corresponding responsibilities have been distributed among the individual alliance members. This results in a concrete need for expenditure – and not solely from a seemingly arbitrary percentage. «It is the plans that dictate our needs, not some pledged ambitions,» said French Admiral Pierre Vandier, Supreme Allied Commander for NATO Transformation, in Brussels in mid-January.

NATO's defense plans and the «Minimum Capability Requirements» set by the High Command are secret, but it has been leaked that the alliance has identified significant gaps. Citing confidential documents from the German Ministry of Defense , the newspaper «Welt am Sonntag» reported as early as October that the number of available combat brigades (of around 5,000 troops) is to increase from 82 to 131, and the number of division headquarters from 24 to 38.

Air defense is considered a particularly weak point. NATO has apparently calculated that with currently available resources, it could only defend five percent of its eastern flank . Given the backdrop of the Russian air war against Ukraine, not only with missiles but also with a growing number of kamikaze drones, such a finding is highly significant. The German Bundeswehr, in particular, has been weakened – at the end of the Cold War, it had 36 Patriot air defense batteries; today, it has only 9, and of those, only 6 are operational in Germany.

Time is of the essence for NATO. The question is what the collective defense shield should look like on land, at sea, in the air, in cyberspace, and in outer space, and whether each alliance member will contribute its share. These discussions have not ended with the recent NATO summit and the agreement on higher spending targets.
This article is an updated version of a previously published text.
